meta_title: Put VpnHood! SERVER Behind a Reverse Proxy Such as Cloudflare | VpnHood!
meta_description: Server IP blocked? Put VpnHood! SERVER behind a reverse proxy such as Cloudflare, on a managed server or a standalone one, and know what the proxy sees.
title: Put your server behind a reverse proxy
lead: A network that blocks your server's IP address cannot stop apps that do not connect to it. Behind a reverse proxy such as Cloudflare, apps connect to the proxy, and the proxy passes the connection on to your server.
how_proxy: Your domain leads to the proxy instead of your server. Apps look the domain up and connect to the proxy, which decrypts the connection, as it does for any website it serves, and encrypts it again toward your server. Their traffic goes over WebSocket, which Cloudflare passes on. Another reverse proxy works too, if it passes WebSocket on and reaches your server over TLS.
diagram_title: Apps reach your server through the proxy
diagram_desc: Your users' apps look up your domain and connect to the reverse proxy, such as Cloudflare, which passes the connection on to your server. The direct route to your server's IP address is blocked, and the apps go around it.
diagram_caption: The proxy gets apps past the block
how_reach: Apps look the domain up only if their key carries it as a trusted name, which takes a certificate from a certificate authority.
how_keys: A key can carry your server's own address as well. Apps then connect either way: the proxy keeps them connected if the address is blocked, but anyone holding the key can read the address. A key without your server's address sends every app through the proxy.
limit_block: Blocking: A network can still block the reverse proxy's addresses, or your domain. Cloudflare's addresses serve many other websites, though, so blocking them has a cost.
limit_dns: DNS: Apps look your domain up through the network's DNS before they connect. If the network blocks or falsifies the answer, apps fall back to the addresses in their key, so a key that carries only the domain cannot connect.
limit_private: Privacy: The reverse proxy sees what is inside the tunnel, just as your server does: where your users connect, and anything they send unencrypted. Their HTTPS stays encrypted. Use a reverse proxy you trust.
limit_tcp: TCP only: Your server does not offer its UDP and QUIC ports to apps that come through the proxy.
limit_terms: Terms: Check that your provider's terms allow VPN traffic. A small group of users, around 50 or fewer, is usually fine.
req_cert: A domain or a subdomain, with a certificate from a certificate authority on your server: Use a domain name and a trusted certificate shows how. Do that first, while the domain's record still points straight at the server.
req_one_server: A single server behind the domain. Records that lead to two servers can send the connections of one session to both, and the session breaks.
req_port: The server listening on TCP port [server_port], or on another port the proxy passes on. Cloudflare passes HTTPS on [cloudflare_https_ports] only.
proxy_record: In Cloudflare, open your domain's DNS records and set the one that points at your server to [cloudflare_proxied], and its AAAA record too if it has one.
proxy_ssl: Under [cloudflare_ssl_tls], set the encryption mode to [cloudflare_full_strict]. Cloudflare then reaches your server over TLS and checks its certificate. In [cloudflare_flexible] mode it would use plain HTTP, which the server does not accept.
proxy_renew: VpnHood! MANAGER renews its certificates over plain HTTP on TCP port [port_http], through the domain, and Cloudflare passes that on to your server. On a managed server, leave [cloudflare_always_https] off: it would redirect the request to HTTPS, and the renewal would fail.
mgr_cert: Check the farm's certificate for the domain: under [manager_signature] it reads [manager_ca_signed], and its [manager_visibility] is [manager_public_in_token]. Keys then carry the domain, and apps look it up.
mgr_hide: To send every app through the proxy, take the server's own addresses out of the keys, in the server's [manager_access_points]:
mgr_step_mode: Edit each address, and set its [manager_mode] to [manager_private].
mgr_step_listen: Leave its [manager_listen] at [manager_yes], so the server keeps listening: the proxy still connects to it.
shot_alt: The Access Points of a server in VpnHood! MANAGER, set for a reverse proxy: Automatic Configuration off (1), and each address with Mode Private (2) and Listen Yes (3)
shot_caption: Both of the server's addresses are out of the keys, and the server still listens on them.
mgr_hide_ca: MANAGER allows keys without an address only while the certificate reads [manager_ca_signed]. Set your server's IP addresses explains each setting.
mgr_keep: Left at [manager_public_in_token], the addresses stay in the keys, and apps use them and the proxy alike. The proxy then keeps your users connected when an address is blocked.
mgr_keys: Apps holding an older key get the new one the next time they connect, as [manager_push_token] is on by default.
mgr_farm: The domain leads to one server, so in a farm of several servers, every app that comes through the proxy reaches the same one.
file_cert: Check that the server uses the domain's certificate, with [setting_is_valid_host_name] set to [json_true]: Use a domain name and a trusted certificate shows how. Keys made since then carry the domain, and apps look it up.
file_keys: A standalone server always puts its own addresses in its keys, beside the domain, so apps use them and the proxy alike. The proxy keeps your users connected when an address is blocked, but anyone holding a key can read the address.
